damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Diagon Alley / Borgin & Burkes back courtyard
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Draco's Borgin & Burkes visit as a solo, clandestine mission he slipped away from his mother to conduct. He browses the shop alone, intimidates Borgin with veiled threats about Fenrir Greyback, demands Borgin keep an item safe, and leaves looking 'very pleased with himself.' The scene establishes his cunning, his independence from Narcissa, and his use of Dark connections as leverage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces this with a mysterious Dark ceremony in the back courtyard of Borgin & Burkes, attended by Narcissa, Bellatrix, and Greyback, in which Draco extends his arm over a cauldron that explodes with light — implying his Dark Mark branding happens here, in company, as a group ritual. Narcissa is present rather than absent. There is no solo intimidation of Borgin, no demonstration of cunning leverage, no pleased self-satisfaction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is critical for establishing Draco as independently dangerous and resourceful — he slips away from his mother, operates alone, and uses sophisticated social intimidation. The film converts this into a passive group ceremony, stripping him of agency and initiative. His solo competence, which is foundational to Harry's suspicion and to the reader's evolving assessment of Draco, is entirely removed. The intimidation of Borgin — including the Greyback threat — which later pays off narratively, is absent.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Hogwarts Express compartment / Petrificus Totalus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Malfoy deliver 'That's from my father' before stamping on Harry's nose — a line that connects the act of cruelty directly to Lucius, framing it as a proxy act of vengeance and establishing Draco's deep investment in family honor and the humiliation of his father's imprisonment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Malfoy stamp on Harry's nose and say 'Oh, right, she was dead before you could wipe the drool off your chin' — a taunting reference to Lily Potter — before covering him with the cloak and saying 'Enjoy the ride back to London.' The 'That's from my father' line and its emotional charge are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The omission of 'That's from my father' removes the explicit link between Draco's cruelty and his loyalty to and grief over his father's imprisonment. The book line makes the violence a family act, deepening Draco's characterisation as someone whose worst impulses are entangled with filial devotion. Without it, the film's Draco is simply casually cruel, losing the specific motivational texture the books build.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Hogwarts Express compartment / Malfoy's boasting to Pansy and Zabini
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has a lengthy, richly observed eavesdropping scene in which Harry hides in the luggage rack and hears Malfoy dismiss Slughorn's Slug Club ('What's it matter to me if some fat old has-been likes me or not?'), speculate openly about not returning to Hogwarts, hint at 'bigger and better things,' and say 'When the Dark Lord takes over, is he going to care how many OWLs anyone's got?' He is performing bravado for Pansy and Zabini, but the scene is also full of suppressed anxiety — Crabbe and Goyle 'gawping,' Malfoy's smirk only 'the ghost of a smirk.' It establishes his pride, his resentment at being excluded from Slughorn's circle, and his ambivalent swagger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses this to a brief exchange where Malfoy says he'd 'pitch himself off the Astronomy Tower' rather than continue at Hogwarts for two more years and hints cryptically that Pansy won't be seeing him in Charms next year. The rich ideological content — his dismissal of OWLs, his Dark Lord loyalty talk, his wounded pride over Slughorn — is stripped away. The Zabini dynamic and the Slug Club resentment are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's train scene does triple duty: it advances Harry's suspicion, characterises Draco's ideology and wounded pride, and subtly shows his anxiety beneath the bravado. The film reduces this to a vague cryptic hint. The loss of the Slughorn exclusion thread in particular damages Draco's characterisation as someone navigating status hierarchies and feeling snubbed — a dimension of his arc that the film never recovers.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Hogwarts Express compartment / Malfoy discovers Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Malfoy uses genuine detective work to identify Harry — he recalls hearing Goyle's trunk hit something, notices a white trainer flash past, and forms a deliberate plan to wait until the compartment is empty before checking. He is shown as perceptive and methodical.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film short-circuits this: Malfoy simply senses the bag on the luggage rack teetering and, after the compartment empties, immediately fires Petrificus Totalus at the rack without the same deliberate investigative reasoning shown in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but present: the book's version gives Draco a moment of genuine cleverness and methodical thinking. The film's version makes it more instinctive and opportunistic. A small reduction in the evidence that Draco is sharper than he is usually credited.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Slughorn's Christmas party corridor / Snape-Malfoy confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's eavesdropped Snape-Malfoy corridor confrontation is long and psychologically rich: Malfoy accuses Snape of trying to steal his glory, refuses Snape's help with contempt and resentment, reveals he's using Occlumency taught by Bellatrix, says 'I've got a plan and it's going to work,' insists 'I've got other people on my side, better people,' and is explicitly angry that Snape put Crabbe and Goyle in detention. The exchange shows Draco's paranoia, his desperate pride in the mission, his distrust of Snape, and his precarious emotional state under enormous pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film version (which is retained in the theatrical cut) is radically condensed. Malfoy says 'I don't need protection. I was chosen for this! Out of all others. Me! And I won't fail him.' Snape says he's afraid; Malfoy insists 'This is my moment!' and exits. The Occlumency detail, the glory-stealing accusation, the Crabbe/Goyle detention grievance, the layered paranoia, and the specific plan references are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is the closest readers get to Draco's interior before the Tower. His complex mixture of pride, paranoia, resentment, and desperation is fully on display. The film reduces him to a single note — chosen-one pride — losing the psychological texture that makes his eventual breakdown on the Tower emotionally coherent. The film's Malfoy seems naively confident rather than desperately clinging to an identity.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Room of Requirement / Vanishing Cabinet work (montage scenes)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The books track Draco's deterioration across the year through Harry's observations: the gray skin, dark shadows, gaunt look, missed Quidditch, skipped prefect duties, and obsessive seclusion. Crucially, Harry also notices 'none of the swagger he had on the Hogwarts Express... The mission, whatever it was, was going badly.' The portrait is of a boy cracking under impossible pressure, showing visible physical and psychological deterioration that makes the Tower scene's emotional weight credible.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does show Draco looking pale and haunted in glimpsed shots — the window scene during the Christmas party, the moonlit corridor with the apple, the Room of Requirement cabinet work sequences. Hermione even comments 'He looks different, don't you think? Almost... ill.' However, these are largely visual and atmospheric rather than characterised through observed behavior and internal logic. The film cuts the scene where Harry specifically reflects on the deterioration as evidence the mission is going badly.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film preserves the visual deterioration but loses the interpretive framework Harry provides — the inference that Draco's decline is the direct result of the mission going badly, that his swagger is gone, that he is a boy out of his depth. Without this framing, the visual pallor reads as atmosphere rather than as a coherent arc of psychological disintegration. The emotional logic of the Tower scene is weakened.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's bathroom scene begins with Harry discovering Malfoy crying at the sink — 'No one can help me. I can't do it. It won't work. And unless I do it soon, he says he'll kill me.' Moaning Myrtle is actively comforting him. The scene reveals Draco's complete psychological collapse: he is openly weeping, shaking, and confessing helplessness before he ever sees Harry. This is a defining moment of vulnerability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core of this scene — Malfoy crying at the mirror, Harry entering, the duel. However, Moaning Myrtle's comforting role and Draco's spoken confession of helplessness ('I can't do it... he'll kill me') are absent from the film's theatrical version. Malfoy is shown crying but the verbal articulation of his fear and impossibility is not present in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's bathroom scene is the emotional hinge of Draco's arc in HBP — the moment where his internal terror is finally externalised in words, not just appearance. The film shows the tears but removes the spoken confession that explains them. Without 'he'll kill me' being stated, the scene is visually present but motivationally opaque, and the Tower scene's 'I've got to kill you or he'll kill me' has less antecedent emotional grounding.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Astronomy Tower / Dumbledore confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Tower scene is an extended negotiation. Dumbledore presses Draco on the details of his plan, praising his ingenuity, while Draco responds to the praise and is drawn into explaining himself — revealing the Vanishing Cabinets, Rosmerta under Imperius, the enchanted coins, ideas borrowed from Dumbledore's Army and Hermione. Dumbledore explicitly tells him his attempts were 'feeble' and wonders aloud if Draco's heart was in them. Draco insists 'It has been in it!' He also explicitly sneers that Snape will 'wake up tomorrow and it'll all be over and he won't be the Dark Lord's favourite any more.' The scene shows Draco drawn out by flattery, desperate for validation, and conflicted.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Tower scene is significantly compressed. Draco reveals the Vanishing Cabinets but the detailed exposition about Rosmerta, the coins, and the borrowed ideas is cut. The key exchange where Dumbledore calls the assassination attempts 'feeble' is present but shorter. Draco's 'He trusts me! I was chosen!' and revealing the Dark Mark are present. The Snape-glory-stealing motivation is absent. The film Draco is confrontational but the layered psychology — his need for praise, his resentment of Snape, his desperation for validation — is compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Tower scene is where every thread of Draco's arc pays off: his pride, his paranoia about Snape stealing glory, his susceptibility to Dumbledore's praise, his moral hesitation. The film preserves the hesitation but loses several of the motivational threads that make it resonant. Specifically, Draco's competitive obsession with Snape — the 'he won't be the Dark Lord's favourite any more' line — is absent, removing a key dimension of why the mission matters to Draco personally beyond survival.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Post-Tower / Harry's reflection on Draco
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book ends with Harry reflecting: 'He did not believe that Malfoy would have killed Dumbledore. He despised Malfoy still for his infatuation with the Dark Arts, but now the tiniest drop of pity mingled with his dislike.' And: 'What was Voldemort making him do under threat of killing him and his parents?' This is the book's explicit, narratively weighted conclusion on Draco's arc in HBP — a shift from pure antagonism to a complex, grudging partial sympathy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry tell Hermione on the Tower: 'No. He was lowering his wand. In the end, it was Snape. It was always Snape.' This acknowledges Draco's hesitation but frames it primarily as evidence about Snape rather than as a moment of reckoning with Draco as a character. The internal pity Harry develops for Draco — explicit in the book — is not voiced or dramatised in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing reflection on Draco is the culmination of his arc in HBP and the seed of the more complex relationship that develops in Deathly Hallows. The film's post-Tower material focuses the emotional resolution on Snape rather than Draco. The 'tiniest drop of pity' — which signals a real shift in Harry's moral landscape regarding his rival — is lost, reducing Draco's arc to one of operational antagonist rather than tragic figure.

main_damage_causes: Compression and replacement of Draco's solo agency moments (Borgin & Burkes, train eavesdropping, Snape corridor confrontation) strips him of the independent cunning and layered psychology that make his arc coherent

Loss of explicit motivational articulation across key scenes (the bathroom confession, the Snape glory-stealing obsession, Harry's closing pity) leaves Draco's internal conflict visually implied but narratively unanchored
The film's post-Tower emotional resolution centres on Snape rather than completing Draco's arc, preventing the 'tiniest drop of pity' shift that is essential groundwork for Deathly Hallows
